clue.text: Anxiously renew mousetraps in English seaside town

indicators.note: something done anxiously is done in a flustered, jumbled way, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone frets about refreshing the mousetraps somewhere on the English coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anxiously' rearranges RENEW MOUSETRAPS. WESTON-SUPER-MARE is a seaside resort in Somerset, on England's Bristol Channel coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Weston-super-Mare is a traditional holiday resort on the Somerset coast of England, so it is an example of such a town.

clue.text: Ancient Greek conflict involving sausages?

definitions.meaning: the naval clash of 480 BC in which the Greek fleet beat the Persians off an island near Athens
read literally, a fight conducted with salamis, the spicy Italian sausages

explanation.surface: A history question about a classical war oddly turns into one about cured meats.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second reading: salamis as the plural of salami.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous sea fight of 480 BC is named after an island; whimsically, the name also describes a skirmish waged with spiced Italian sausages.

clue.text: Dear fellow involved in a fine romance

parts.note: a term of endearment, like 'love' when addressing someone

indicators.note: being involved in something means sitting within it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: fine weather is fair weather

explanation.surface: A dear man gets caught up in a splendid courtship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved in' places the fellow between the article and the word for fine, a container that sits after the term of endearment.
explanation.definitionFit: A romance is a relationship of passion between two people, the same sense as an amorous liaison.

clue.text: Attempt to describe people in fine detail

indicators.note: to describe here is to draw a line around, so the attempt encloses the people

parts.note: to attempt is to try
a race is a people or nation

explanation.surface: Someone tries to give an intricate account of a group of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to describe' is used in its geometric sense of drawing a line round a shape, which is why the attempt encloses the people.
explanation.definitionFit: Tracery is the delicate ornamental stonework in Gothic windows, an example of intricate decorative work.

clue.text: It pains one to embrace husband

indicators.note: embracing means holding something within one's arms, so the one wraps round the husband

parts.note: an ace is the card counting as one
H is the abbreviation for husband in genealogy and records

explanation.surface: It hurts somebody to have to hug their spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to embrace' puts H inside ACE. 'It' is part of the surface only: 'It aches' matches 'It pains'.
explanation.definitionFit: To ache is to hurt or throb with discomfort, so 'pains' as a verb is a synonym.

clue.text: "Spurn Napoleon or suffer!" they say

indicators.note: the letters are made to suffer, mangled into a different arrangement

explanation.surface: A rallying cry threatening the French emperor with pain if he is rejected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suffer!' rearranges SPURN NAPOLEON OR. 'they say' means 'they, for example': the word 'they' is one of these grammatical items.
explanation.definitionFit: The word 'they' is a classic grammatical item standing in for people, so it serves as an example of the category.

clue.text: Suggesting London could be providing goods, money etc

definitions.meaning: a whimsical picture of the capital city drifting loose on the water
in finance, capital held in circulating form such as stock, cash and goods rather than fixed assets

explanation.surface: An economics definition prefaced by a fanciful image of the British capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'providing' links the two readings. One sense is the financial term; the other imagines a capital city that floats.
explanation.definitionFit: Economists call capital in circulation, such as cash, stock and goods in transit, by this term, as opposed to fixed assets like buildings.

clue.text: Harp on about "Blue Boar", Barking

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters go crazy and rearrange

explanation.surface: A pub called the Blue Boar in the London district of Barking is endlessly talked about.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking looks like the east London district (or a dog's noise) but is the anagram signal, British slang for 'mad'; it rearranges BLUE BOAR.
explanation.definitionFit: To belabour a point is to dwell on it at excessive length, which is what harping on about something means.

clue.text: Cross language and curses regularly used by old American

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals means every other letter of the word

parts.note: ole is the American folksy spelling of 'old', as in 'good ole boy'

explanation.surface: Someone describes a mixed tongue full of swearing spoken by an elderly American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the odd letters of curses, C-R-E; 'used by' attaches the folksy American form of 'old'.
explanation.definitionFit: A creole is a fully developed language formed from a mixture of others, so it is a hybrid or crossbred tongue.

clue.text: It's tasteless to be enthralled by girl's bust, perhaps

indicators.note: being enthralled means being held captive, so the tasteless stuff is held inside the girl

parts.note: Sue is a girl's name
tat is cheap, tasteless stuff

explanation.surface: A sculpted bust of a girl is dismissed as kitsch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be enthralled by' means held captive inside. A bust is one kind of sculpture, hence the 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bust is a sculpted head and shoulders, one kind of carved or cast figure.

clue.text: Revolutionary guards work for king, say

parts.note: Che Guevara is the archetypal revolutionary
the SS were Hitler's elite guards
to man a post is to staff or work it

explanation.surface: Insurgent bodyguards labour on behalf of a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests rebels serving a monarch, but 'king' is a board-game piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The king is one of the pieces on the chessboard, so it is an example of such a playing piece.

clue.text: Woman unmanned guards

indicators.note: guarding means holding inside, so the name lies within the word

explanation.surface: A woman stands watch over an unstaffed post.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne is a common female first name, so it is an example of a woman.

clue.text: If ignored, a disaster for the world's poorest

definitions.text: If ignored, a disaster for the world's poorest

indicators.note: a disaster leaves things wrecked and scrambled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning that neglecting overseas assistance would be catastrophic for poor countries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disaster' rearranges IF IGNORED A; the whole clue also describes the answer, since neglecting it would hurt the poorest.
explanation.definitionFit: Help given by rich countries to poorer ones is what the whole sentence describes as vital to the world's poorest.

clue.text: Printing opinion

definitions.meaning: a printing is a single print run of a book
a view or feeling formed about something, as in 'my sense of him'

explanation.definitionFit: Publishers call each print run an impression, and an impression is also the view one forms of something.

clue.text: Painful disease recognised retrospectively after George's 1991 conflict

definitions.text: Painful disease recognised retrospectively after George's 1991 conflict

parts.words: Painful disease recognised retrospectively after George's 1991 conflict
parts.note: describes the 1991 war led by President George H W Bush against Iraq, after which veterans' illness was named a syndrome

explanation.surface: A medical-history note about an illness identified among veterans of a 1991 war.
explanation.walkthrough: George is US President George H. W. Bush, who led the coalition to free Kuwait from Iraq in 1991; its veterans' unexplained illnesses were later called a syndrome bearing the war's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1991 campaign to expel Iraq from Kuwait, under the first President Bush, gave its name to an illness found among returning troops.

clue.text: Active gay pens sweet expression of regret

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, so the rearranged letters surround the sweet
an active word is lively and stirred up, so its letters move around

parts.note: taken as written
a Polo is a British mint sweet with a hole

explanation.surface: A lively gay man writes something sugary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Active' stirs the three letters to AGY, and 'pens' wraps them round the sweet; a Polo is a British mint with a hole in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying sorry is the classic way of voicing regret, so a formal statement of remorse fits.

clue.text: Mum's an expert cook

parts.note: Ma is mum, with the possessive s kept as a letter
a sage is a wise person or expert

explanation.surface: A child boasts that their mother is a skilled chef.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cook' is a verb here, as in 'cook the books': nothing to do with the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: To cook figures is to falsify them, and to massage statistics means the same, a fiddling sense.

clue.text: Irishman trapped in Eritrea struggling to get transport home

indicators.note: being trapped in something means being held inside it
struggling suggests writhing about, so these letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: Pat (Patrick) is the stock Irishman's name

explanation.surface: An Irishman stuck in war-torn Eritrea tries to arrange his journey back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'struggling' makes RERIATE, and 'trapped in' wraps it round the Irishman; Pat, short for Patrick, is the stock Irish name.
explanation.definitionFit: To repatriate someone is to send them back to their own country, which is transporting them home.

clue.text: Fancy rare breed

indicators.note: fancy is used in the sense of elaborately reworked, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An exotic, uncommon type of animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a prized animal breed, but 'breed' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To rear animals is to raise or breed them, a straightforward verb synonym.

clue.text: One's finding ways through insurmountable difficulties

parts.note: 'one's' as 'one is' becomes I'm, said in the first person
passes are routes through mountains

explanation.surface: A person finds routes across terrible obstacles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' is read as 'one is', which a speaker would say as I'M. Mountain passes as ways through suit the 'insurmountable' surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An impasse is a deadlock or situation with no way forward, so the plural means problems that cannot be overcome.

clue.text: Overturn vote in support of huge monocrop

indicators.note: in a down clue, overturning turns the column upside down, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: ay (aye) is a yes vote
OS is the abbreviation for outsize

explanation.surface: Campaigners want to reverse a vote backing a vast single-crop farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overturn' reads AY followed by OS backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Soya beans are often grown over vast areas as a single crop, so they are an example of a monoculture crop.

clue.text: Muslims in North America backing holy man

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
US for the United States of America
S is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: A holy man in North America supports a group of believers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns IN-N-US round to SUNNI; the saint's S follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunnis are members of the larger of the two main branches of Islam, so they are followers of that faith.

clue.text: Clever and original but wet

indicators.note: the original letter of a word is its starting one

parts.note: rainy weather is wet weather

explanation.surface: Someone is smart and inventive, though a bit feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wet' looks like the British sense 'feeble', but means rainy weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Brainy means intelligent, a close synonym of smart or clever.

clue.text: Round Glasgow leaders have reformed Labour

indicators.note: the leading letters of Glasgow are its opening pair
reformed means formed again in a different arrangement, so these letters are reshuffled

explanation.surface: Political news that the Glasgow party bosses have overhauled the Labour Party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaders' takes the first two letters, GL, of Glasgow; 'reformed' rearranges LABOUR to OBULAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Globular means shaped like a ball, a synonym for spherical or round.
